newsitem.title: USA: Guaranteed investments have a role in retirement plans.
newsitem.headline: Guaranteed investments have a role in retirement plans.

text.p: What do you do when you have a product that develops a bad name for itself? Redesign it, rename it, and roll it out again.

That's what the investment industry has done with guaranteed retirement investments, and there are some signs the strategy is working -- both for the industry and those investors who are willing to give these instruments a second chance.

First, a little history: Guaranteed investment contracts or GICs, were big in the early 1980s. They were contracts with insurance companies that promised set amounts of return over set amounts of time. They offered better returns than banks and more stability than bonds. American workers liked what they saw and packed their 401(k) defined-contribution retirement accounts with these instruments. Then, trouble.

As workers became smarter about investing, they learned that greater proportions of their retirement money should be invested for long-term growth in the stock market, and not in guaranteed investments that may have been safe but offered only limited returns. And then it turned out these "guarantees" were less than safe: A couple of insurance companies, Executive Life and Mutual Benefit, defaulted on their GICs. Those defaults, coupled with the boom in stock prices, saw retirement savers abandon GICs in favour of stock and bond mutual funds.
Now, the industry has been reborn, and there are some indications that retirement savers should give it a second chance. The new name for the products are "stable value funds."

Instead of being promises from one insurance company, they tend to be pools of bond investments backed by insurance companies, banks and investment banking firms. Because of this diversification, the risks of default are lower. And because they are carefully managed pools of risk with third-party guarantees, they tend to have less volatility than the bonds of which they are comprised.

What does that mean for investors? A lot, according to retirement plan designers. Wayne Gates, an economist with John Hancock Financial Services, recently studied the effects of stable value products on various retirement portfolios. He found that investors who use stable value products to balance the stock funds in their retirement accounts could actually bump up their stock holdings and therefore, their returns, without giving up safety.

According to Gates, these stable value investments are less volatile than bonds. So an investor who built a portfolio of 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds could instead use only 29 percent stable value funds and 71 percent stocks to achieve the same risk levels. The performance bonus, said Gates, would be better than half a percentage point in annual returns.

Over the last 12 years, the first portfolio would have earned 14 percent; the second one 14.6 percent. If those returns held steady, the investor who put away $10,000 could earn $2,000 more every 10 years by avoiding bonds and instead building a portfolio of stock and stable value funds.

What's the lesson for today's 401(k) holder? If you're still entirely in guaranteed investments, diversify into stock mutual funds. If you moved entirely out of guaranteed investments but substituted bonds instead, consider a small move back into the guarantees.
They may buy you more bang with less bucking and weaving.
